intro: Sport is also work. A college player sits in class in the morning and appears on national television at night. A professional player signs a contract that says where they may live and play. For more than 150 years, athletes, owners, colleges, courts and unions have argued over who controls a player's time, name and career.

This unit reads that argument through real papers: a railroad's offer in 1852, the Western Conference rules written in Chicago in 1895, the reserve agreement of 1879, John Montgomery Ward's 1887 essay, Supreme Court rulings from 1922 to 2021, an arbitrator's decision in 1975 and a labor board ruling in Chicago in 2014.

By the end, you will be able to explain what eligibility rules, the reserve clause and free agency are. You can trace how television money changed college sport. You can also compare how courts, unions and lawmakers each changed the rules, and argue from dated documents about who should own a career.
bigQuestion: Who should control an athlete's time, name and career: the school, the club or the athlete?

timeline.t: Harvard and Yale row the first intercollegiate race, paid for by a railroad
William Hulbert of Chicago leads the founding of the National League
National League owners agree to reserve five players each
Players form the Players' League for one season
The Western Conference, later the Big Ten, is founded in Chicago
The IAAUS, renamed the NCAA in 1910, is founded
Supreme Court gives baseball an antitrust exemption
Arbitrator Peter Seitz rules for Messersmith and McNally
Supreme Court ends the NCAA's football television plan
Congress passes the Curt Flood Act
NCAA v. Alston decided; college players may earn NIL money

words.d: the rules that decide who is allowed to play
school aid given because a student plays a sport, allowed by the NCAA from 1956
the legal right, sold for money, to show an event
laws that forbid businesses from joining together to limit competition
the NCAA's term for a college player, stressing school first
name, image and likeness; money a player earns from their identity
a contract paragraph that let a club renew a player's contract year after year
a player's right to sign with any club once a contract ends
a neutral person both sides agree will decide a dispute

test.q: Who paid for the 1852 Harvard–Yale regatta?
test.why: A railroad paid the crews' costs, hoping to draw passengers.

test.q: What city hosted the 1895 founding of the Western Conference?
test.why: University presidents met at the Palmer House in Chicago.

test.q: What was the 1929 Carnegie report about?
choices: Recruiting and secret subsidies in college sport
test.why: American College Athletics documented recruiting and subsidies.

test.q: What did the NCAA allow for the first time in 1956?
test.why: From 1956 schools could give aid for athletic ability.

test.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in the 1984 Board of Regents case?
choices: The NCAA's football TV plan broke antitrust law
Baseball is exempt from antitrust law
test.why: The Court ruled 7 to 2 that the TV plan restrained trade.

test.q: In which city did a labor board official rule in 2014 that Northwestern football players were employees?
test.why: The NLRB regional director in Chicago issued the 2014 ruling.

test.q: What did the reserve clause let a club do?
choices: Renew a player's contract year after year
test.why: Owners read the renewal paragraph as binding a player to the club indefinitely.

test.q: Who wrote Is the Base Ball Player a Chattel? in 1887?
test.why: Ward, a player and lawyer, published it in Lippincott's Magazine.

test.q: Why did Federal Baseball (1922) matter for decades?
choices: It gave baseball an antitrust exemption
It ended the Federal League's park
test.why: Holmes held baseball was not interstate commerce, so antitrust law did not apply.

test.q: How did the Curt Flood Act relate to Flood v. Kuhn?
choices: Congress acted where the 1972 Court said Congress should decide
test.why: The Court left the change to Congress, which passed the act in 1998.

test.q: What did arbitrator Peter Seitz decide in 1975?
choices: The renewal paragraph bound a player for only one extra year
test.why: Seitz ruled that Messersmith and McNally were free after their renewal year.

test.q: How did the collusion of the 1980s echo the 1879 reserve agreement?
choices: In both, owners agreed not to compete for players
Both were made by players' unions
test.why: In 1879 and in the 1980s, owners agreed among themselves not to bid for players.

test.q: Which statement compares college and pro players correctly before 2021?
choices: Both had unions that signed agreements
Pro players could bargain as a union; college players were called students, not employees
College players were free agents; pro players were not
Both were paid NIL money by rule
test.why: Pro unions bargained from 1968, while the NCAA treated players as student-athletes.

test.q: What did NCAA v. Alston (2021) decide?
choices: The NCAA could not cap education-related benefits
test.why: The Court ruled 9 to 0 against caps on education-related benefits.

test.q: What was the Bosman ruling of 1995?
choices: A European court decision freeing out-of-contract soccer players
test.why: The European Court of Justice ruled for Jean-Marc Bosman on December 15, 1995.

write.prompt: Who should control an athlete's career? Argue your answer using at least three dated documents from this unit, such as the 1879 reserve agreement, Ward's 1887 essay, Federal Baseball (1922), the Seitz decision (1975) or NCAA v. Alston (2021). Say what each says and how each side read it.
tips: Name each document with its date and who wrote or decided it.
Explain each side's view fairly before you judge it.
Compare a college case with a professional case.
Use unit terms such as reserve clause, free agency, antitrust and eligibility.
